newsitem.title: USA: Kasich sees Congress, Clinton avoiding shutdown.
newsitem.headline: Kasich sees Congress, Clinton avoiding shutdown.

text.p: The Republican-led Congress and President Clinton will likely put their differences aside and reach agreement on a 1998 budget, avoiding another government shutdown, House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich said Saturday.

Kasich told CNN's "Evans & Novak" programme he had heard the budget Clinton would present to Congress in February did not include military reform, efforts to solve the problems of Medicare, or any change in measuring the cost-of-living index.

But he declined to call it a "sham" budget, saying: "Those are just rumours and I hope that they're going to be more serious about this and that we can at least sit down and work something decent out."

Kasich said Clinton and the Republicans still had differences over the budget, but he did not believe that fighting over it would result in another shutdown like the one that kept federal workers home in December 1995.

"I don't anticipate us getting into these kinds of wars again because they're too difficult to explain to the American people about really what's at stake," Kasich said. "And we're going to do a better job in terms of explaining what we're doing but at the end of the day my sense is we'll have to reach some kind of agreement."
"I hope that the budget they send first of all is better than the rumours I'm hearing,' Kasich said, adding that negotiations would begin once the budget was submitted.

Kasich said he would continue his efforts to cut so-called corporate welfare, or tax subsidies and benefits for companies, saying various groups from the political left and right had met to discuss the issue at his suggestion.
The groups had reached agreement on "about 12 items that they think that the left and the right can go to eliminate in spending," Kasich said, without giving details on the items.
He said Republicans would not press ahead with adjustments to the cost of living index if the administration refused.

"If the administration said they're going to veto major policy changes, there isn't a lot of sense in sending it down there and having the president veto something and then run around and beat us over the head with a club for political reasons. So we're going to be smarter this time," he said.
Kasich said he expected the budget to include tax cuts, although he hoped they would be permanent, resulting both in capital gain tax reductions and a break for middle-income families.
